speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I welcome the policy change to allow for fathers to take two weeks' paid paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, let me declare my interest as a board member of the Centre for Fathering.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I have been there for over 12 years now.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This reinforces shared parenting responsibilities and the increasing role that fathers play in families.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore has been on a trajectory to increase the provision of maternity leave and, sometimes, this can be perceived to be at the expense of the women's career prospects.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister tell us how it intends to recalibrate existing policies to keep up with changing realities on child-rearing?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I know that in asking this question, I am posing this "having the cake and eat it" scenario.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But I do think that it is a false choice that we present to women today – between leaning in and keeling over at work, as one recent mother wrote in the papers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To do this, we need more support for fathers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The presence and active involvement of a father leads to children more likely to do well in school, have healthy self-esteem and avoid high-risk behaviours, compared with children who are raised without a father.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: While society has prepared women for the workforce, we have not prepared fathers to be involved with their children.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As a nation, we need to consider fathering education as a core support to prepare men to be fathers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: While NS training prepares them for national defence, their future role as involved fathers prepares them for social defence, in making homes a safe haven for children.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: When these men become first-time fathers, a basic course on fathering can make a significant difference in raising awareness of the crucial roles they play and provide some basic tools for involved fatherhood.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Young children with fathers who are incarcerated are deprived of the important bonding they could have.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The longer they are apart, the harder it is to regain the bond and that increases risk of child neglect.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Such fathers need to be given a chance to bond with their children through special programmes for incarcerated fathers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Such bonding, though necessarily limited because of circumstances, is not only precious in itself, but also increases the motivation of these fathers to stay out of trouble for their family.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is time to recognise the difference fathers can make in teenagers who are at a crucial stage of transition into adulthood.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to encourage better fathering for these teens.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Many research studies indicate that the quality of the relationship between the child's parents is the central engine governing the healthy functioning Page: 79 of the family system.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to consider funding marriage enrichment training for couples during crucial times, such as just before the arrival of the first born, just before the teen years, and when parents are incarcerated.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to provide incentives for fathers to be involved with their school-going children by giving them time-off to be at school.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We must recognise companies who are father-friendly, companies who consider involved fathering as a leadership quality that will positively impact their team.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Parenting and working is a balance that each one of us – mothers or fathers, men and women, sisters and brothers – we all have to decide for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This decision, however, is made in a context and within societal and national norms.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Government has a big role in the formation of these norms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I am concerned about the manpower adequacy in these centres.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am also aware that the Ministry has expanded student intakes, introduced Professional Conversion Programmes and enhanced career progression opportunities in a bid to attract and retain early childhood educators.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One particular development which I must commend is the greater number of childcare centres set up at workplaces.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This means greater convenience and peace of mind for Page: 80 more parents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Minister share with us the key areas where improvements in the childcare sector have been made?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How does MSF intend to build on these achievements in the next few years?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   There are many young parents living in Punggol.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of the young mothers would like to return to work as soon as possible after giving birth.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, in order to return to work, they have to send their children to childcare centres.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The problem is, one needs to queue on a waitlist for a place at the childcare centre.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is because the development of childcare centres has hit a bottleneck: it is difficult to recruit teachers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Because the Government has laid out many requirements for early childhood educators.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, for a preschooler, what she needs most is to learn through real-life experiences, to learn through play.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She does not necessarily need a sophisticated learning system.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What she needs is love, companionship and encouragement.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, can we consider lowering the criteria for childcare teachers, so that more caring individuals with experience in taking care of children can be recruited?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In this way, we can increase the number of teachers and more children can receive care.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, can we consider setting up community-based parent support centres at the RC centres and allow housewives with experience and time to take care of children in need?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Government draw up relevant safety standards and establish a feasible model based on mutual support within the community?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the past, when there were big families, children could be taken care of by relatives after they were born.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But, nowadays, couples only have each other within the family, and raising children becomes more difficult.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, as the saying goes, "远亲不如近邻", meaning that a neighbour who is near is better than a relative who lives far away.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In terms of early childhood education, can we take in more caring individuals, promote mutual support within the neighbourhood and lighten the load of young parents?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They are naturally eager for knowledge and some children require a very structured teacher-led style of learning while others learn better in a child-led environment that emphasises individuality and creativity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is the responsibility of parents to assess the temperament and learning abilities of their children and to select the most appropriate school and curriculum for their children's growth and development.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, the unevenness of KiFAS means that the choices that they make for their children's education are limited, especially for the less well-off.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Kindergarten education is extremely important as it sets the foundation for skills that they will build on later in life and plays an important role in the social and emotional growth of the child.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: KiFAS can currently only be used in about half of all registered kindergartens which are in the centres run by anchor operators and MOE.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This stifles competition with other operators that provide quality education but are not KiFAS-eligible and limits parents' choices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But many families are still subjected to escalating fees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To further enhance the supply side stabilisation of fees, could ECDA also ensure that we have enough anchor or partner operators to cater enough childcare places to at least half of each cohort?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, if we plan for a childcare place for every Singaporean child, we can reduce competition for places that drives up fees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I would also like to ask if the Ministry can review its subsidies based on the "true cost" of childcare services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Besides childcare fees, most centres offer enrichment programmes as options.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many parents feel pressured to also enrol for these classes, lest their children are left to play on their own while their peers pick up additional skills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry do a nationwide study to find out what percentage of parents are taking up these enrichment courses for their children at such centres?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If most of the children are already doing so, are these options truly "optional"?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have to be mindful not to introduce inequality into the education system to the very young children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can only imagine the impact on the child who has to sit out enrichment classes because his parents are not able to afford them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the childcare fees of the centres are stated on the ECDA website, could the Ministry consider mandating that childcare operators do state the full cost of their services, including enrichment or optional classes, online on their websites or in publicity materials, so parents will know what they are in for?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The situation gets even tougher when both parents are working.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Many parents are faced with the delicate balance of managing both work and family.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For those who are single parents, the stress they are facing is even greater.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, they are emotionally affected due to problems at work or in their family.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There are surveys and reports that suggest that there is a Page: 82 correlation between single motherhood and depression.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: During an interview in 2014, Harry Potter author JK Rowling talked about how, when she was a single mother, she was so depressed that she considered suicide but was saved by thoughts of her daughter.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, it would be worth exploring the possibility of linking every company within a geographical location to the social service network, such as Social Service Centre or Family Service Centre.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With such collaborative efforts, companies can assist the worker with the appropriate help which may not be available at the workplace.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Such small but meaningful effort goes a long way for the individual worker's mental and emotional stability.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Our dependence on this group of Singaporeans is real, substantial and often unacknowledged.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In many ways, informal or unpaid caregivers enable other Singaporeans to carry out the economic activities reckoned in our GDP, while their own caregiving is not.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: As of now, the burden of informal caregiving falls disproportionately on women.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: As noted in this House before, it is well-documented that caregivers often suffer declines in their own financial circumstances and mental and physical health.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Often, these caregivers pass up opportunities, stay at home and can find themselves with little support and resources for their own retirement or care.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Other examples of a much-needed acknowledgement and support for caregivers could include the leave for caregivers that several Members of this House have called for, or greater support for working informal caregivers when they exercise their rights to ask for flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Page: 83 Education and home environment are important for such upward socioeconomic mobility.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Whilst we have a good education system in Singapore, we need to help the less-advantaged children benefit fully from it.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Sadly, a home environment – where there is non-parental involvement, poor home literacy and unmotivated parents who do not send their children to school – sets the children back.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to improve the home environment for these families.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Studies have shown that a less-advantaged family background or socioeconomic status affects the likelihood of students graduating from high school or college.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, there is a need to identify this group for early intervention.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Most times, these families have low skills and low-paying jobs and may have a slew of needs, such as in housing, income, childcare or ill-health of family members.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The parents of such families need to acquire long-term capabilities, such as upgrading of skills and job placement.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The mothers have to move away from prejudices and mental barriers to employment.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Their children should be assisted with their well-being, daily care, healthcare and education.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: More social workers and MSF staff are required to undertake such a hands-on personalised approach to solve the various needs of each family.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Most times, many of their issues cannot be solved overnight and these families may require long-term follow-up.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes, the foreign spouse may also have a non-Singaporean child from a previous marriage who is here on a Student Pass.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This parent has to make a decision whether to stay in Singapore or to move back to his or her home country.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some went on to start a family with their child born in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For some, the Singaporean spouse is usually the sole breadwinner.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The issue becomes complicated when the spouse passes away, becomes handicapped or critically ill, is jailed, or when the couple undergoes divorce.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The foreign spouse suddenly has to take on the responsibility to support the family and their young children.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am not sure of the residential status of the mother, but I am sure it is a challenging circumstance for the family.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For such families, it is most unfortunate that they have to be put through such difficult circumstances.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of these foreign spouses are here on social visit passes, Long-Term Visit Pass or Long-Term Visit Pass-Plus (LTVP or LTVP+).

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For some of them, they can work if they have a Letter of Consent.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If not, they may have to leave the country with their children back to their home country.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does the Ministry have figures on the number of children who are impacted under such circumstances?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What assistance can we offer to ensure that the children grow up in a supportive Page: 84 environment?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can we provide emotional support for the spouse, as well as education needs for the children and their childcare needs?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For such spouses, can we give exemption to allow them to work and to bring up their children here in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Families of all shapes and sizes – they are a key part of my mission, both in Parliament and in my work in the community, especially in the Centre for Fathering, where I serve on the board.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Single-parent families are already socially stigmatised and face more challenges than nuclear households.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Our policies should not create more barriers for them when they seek assistance.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: That will give a clear signal that the Government does not consider their claim to national spending to be any less because of their circumstance, willing or unwilling.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: How can the Government reduce the vulnerabilities that children from single-parent households face?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: In particular, for children of unwed parents – almost always mothers – can we extend GPML to them?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: I have only mentioned GMPL, co-matching for CDA and the CDA First Step grant to benefit single-parent families.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Of course, there is a myriad of policies, not limited to housing or Baby Bonus, that are out of scope for this group but who definitely need them the most.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Single parenting is often not a choice but a result of circumstance.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: I, therefore, repeat my call and ask the Minister to review the current differentials in policies and to recalibrate them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We must continue to give all our young a good and more equalised start in life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Because by doing so, we are also making sure that the future sons and daughters of Singapore start on a good footing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: In Singapore, while all children are precious and should enjoy equal opportunities, some are still "more equal than others".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I feel very much for one group of children and they would be children of single parents, mainly unwed mothers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Page: 85 Firstly, children are innocent and, since they have been given life, we must cherish and nurture them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Give them opportunities and help them blossom into responsible and capable citizens of Singapore and of the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Hence, we must focus our policies and efforts on their well-being.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: This situation is exacerbated if the responsible parent is of lower income.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Therefore, I hope the Ministry will consider the following.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: This move is to allow the mother to have sufficient time to bond with the newborn.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: The child, from the point of birth, was already disadvantaged, having only one parent to rely on.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: It is all the more important for them to have enough time to develop the emotional attachment essential for a stable mother-child relationship.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: This was meant to be a special savings account for children's healthcare and educational expenses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: It is not a normal bank account which parents can frivolously tap on.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Hence, if it is meant to benefit the child, why not allow children of unwed mothers to enjoy it as well?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: First, it encourages the mother to save money for the child.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We should prevent an unnecessary widening of the gap between Singaporean children just because of their parents' marital status.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Given their relative disadvantageous start in life, I sincerely hope that KidSTART will help equalise the learning, developmental and health support these children can receive from the state.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is important for a mother to recuperate physically and emotionally from child bearing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The time a mother can share with her child is especially precious and, when managed well, can strengthen the psychological and emotional bond that a mother shares with her child.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Working mothers often have to quickly get back to work while they are still struggling to find infant care assistance for their child.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the end of the day, a mother's marital status is irrelevant when it comes to the struggles I have just described.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Baby Bonus Scheme was designed to help families defray the costs of raising a child.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It comprises a cash gift and a CDA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The CDA account will certainly come in handy to help the single parent manage early childhood expenses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last week, I asked the Minister for Finance during the Budget debate to confirm whether CDA First Step Grant is available to children of single unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister did not answer this Page: 86 question, preferring to leave this to MSF to deal with in the Committee of Supply debate this week.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are also not eligible for housing subsidies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Single parents need to provide themselves and their children with a roof over their heads, too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current housing policy puts a heavier burden on single parents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are often compelled to rent or purchase from the open market.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With hefty rental rates, they may have to cut back on other expenses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Or they have to stay in an over-crowded flat with other relatives.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The children suffer when there is less money for their own well-being or a less desirable environment for them to grow and learn.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government may think that they are just penalising single parents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But actually, the Government is making life harder for the innocent children of single parents for they have to grow up with more challenges and fewer resources.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This should be about ensuring better and fair support for their children.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These children are Singaporeans, sons will serve National Service and daughters will continue to bear and nurture future generations for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should acknowledge the value that these children will bring to our country, our people and our economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When one sees the value, then the cost becomes insignificant, the stigma becomes unnecessary.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Give these children the same opportunities as others, without the stigma.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government allows singles, whether men or women, to adopt children.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If MSF thinks that it is fine for singles to adopt children, then these adoptive parents and their children should be entitled to the same relevant benefits as married adoptive parents and their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are some benefits that single parents currently do not enjoy, such as the full 16 weeks of maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Unwed parents also do not get perks, such as the Baby Bonus and parenthood tax rebates, and have to wait until they are 35 years old to buy a HDB flat under the singles scheme.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Single parents have a difficult time bringing up their child or children single-handedly, compared to families with two parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As an inclusive society, we should be providing equal rights to single parents and ensure they do not feel alone in their journey.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry, for a start, consider helping single parents by extending the length of maternity leave given to single mothers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry consider providing any other support for single parents?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: All Singaporean sons and daughters should have equal opportunities to succeed, regardless of their origin or birth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: It should be an inalienable right of every Singaporean baby.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Yet, for the children of single unmarried mothers, they are not equals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Thus, they may have four to eight weeks of paid maternity leave less than their lawfully-wedded peers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: These four to eight weeks make a difference.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Women are more likely to breastfeed with the full 16 weeks of maternity leave – bringing with it long-term health and development benefits for the child.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: For the same stated benefits that the children of lawfully-wedded mothers enjoy from these grants, these children are denied.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I understand the need for policies to be signposts of the inclinations and views of the larger society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Yet, would it not also be the societal view that we should support those who are in need?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: It will be difficult to find Singaporeans who do not believe in equal opportunities for our Singaporean sons and daughters, as what many of my fellow Members of Parliament have pointed out.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Therefore, I urge the Government to review if it can extend full maternity benefits to all Singaporean children, regardless of the marital status of their mothers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I also urge the Government to allow unwed mothers tax reliefs under the Working Mothers Child Relief and Foreign Maid Levy Relief – so that the child can benefit from the money saved from paying taxes, and have the support of a domestic worker.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: As lawmakers, let us look into any child's eyes and be filled with love that we have done our best to ensure that he is, indeed, equal amongst peers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Based on statistics released by the Ministry, there has been an increase in the number of child abuse investigations since 2009.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Of the 158 cases, physical abuse was the most common, followed by sexual abuse, physical neglect and emotional abuse.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: I understand that the Ministry has a Child Protection and Welfare Service that coordinates the protection and welfare plans for the child, as well as providing assistance to the family.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: In addition, the Ministry works with VWOs, such as the Singapore Children's Society, TRANS Centre and other Family Service Centres (FSCs), in providing holistic support for the child and the family.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Together with these VWOs, the Ministry has worked to provide and coordinate supportive services that build parenting capacities, alternative care arrangements, early identification of abuse and neglect, as well as substitute services, such as foster family care, adoption and residential care, for the children.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: For example, within the Ministry, there is also the Positive Parenting Programme that teaches positive parenting skills for families.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: There are also recovery programmes for children and adolescents who have experienced sexual abuse, as well as for their non-offending parents and caregivers, to provide them with skills to help their children.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Page: 88 All these are not piecemeal efforts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Yet, there still remain a substantial number of child abuse cases, as seen from the statistics that I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng

text: However, I understand that some of them are subjected to abuse, especially when those who seek help react emotionally.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Currently, there is a wide range of income criteria applied to public service applications from different agencies, ranging from financial assistance to public housing to foreign spouse immigration.

text: The variation can be in the form of gross versus nett, aggregated versus per capita and varying qualifying income ceilings for different but possibly similar schemes.

text: Hence, could the Government consider applying net per capita income as the criterion across the board?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The story of the Singapore Prison Service (SPS) is a very powerful signpost of what can be achieved when the Government matches culture with strategy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In 1988, SPS faced wicked problems – overcrowded prisons, a severe manpower shortage, overworked and discouraged prison officers and lousy public perception.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: That means half the ex-offenders were back into prison within two years of release.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There was also a vicious intergenerational cycle – children of inmates were becoming offenders themselves.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, a small group of SPS leaders dared to ask themselves: how was Singapore Prisons creating security for all if it did not do anything to reduce repeat offences?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: These Page: 90 early adopters pushed through a progressive idea that perhaps the primary job of a prison was not to keep "bad" people in but to get them out forever.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: At the heart of SPS' culture transformation strategy was the repositioning of prison officers as Captains of Lives with a mission to rehabilitate, renew and restart.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And prisoners were repositioned not as problems to control but people worthy of support on a historic quest for redemption.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The prison officer was no longer a gate-keeper that worked on minimising the cost of "bad" people but repositioned as a guide that worked on maximising possibilities for people wanting to do good again.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The public were no longer empathetic bystanders but repositioned as vital participants who could unlock a systemic second prison.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: MHA was sceptical at first and worried that this soft "culture-first" approach would not produce results and waste public money.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I speak at length about the Singapore Prison story because I see important parallels of the on-going struggles we face in the social sector in the struggle against the poverty cycle.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I also see new possibilities in adopting the "culture-as-first-resort" approach pioneered by Singapore Prison.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Right now, many FSCs feel similarly overwhelmed by demand and strained for resources.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many social workers feel burnt out, especially when they see people sunk in poverty, relapsing back into impoverishing behaviours despite intervention after intervention.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many of the poor also expressed demotivation when they − wrongfully or not − perceive their social workers acting more like gatekeepers, working for the good of the system rather than guides working for the good of the people.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Third, what if Fresh Start was not just a housing scheme but the beginning of a whole-of-Government, whole-of-society movement that engaged all stakeholders to work as one to disrupt poverty together?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, what would SkillsFuture for a Fresh Start or Public Broadcasting for a Fresh Start look like?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: As we work on the transformation of how we help our working elite, let us also transform how we help our working poor as well.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Chairman, at my Meet-the-People sessions, I see many elderly residents requesting financial assistance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, a critical measure of our successes as a society is social mobility.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the part of the glue that binds Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have heard from a friend in the social work profession that he has begun seeing clients in need of social work help who are the children of the clients that he saw 20 years ago.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, no one is cheered by stories like these.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOF's Occasional Paper published in 2012 and updated in 2015 suggested that the 1978-1982 cohort and 1974-1978 cohort saw an inter-generational mobility measure of around 0.2, which is relatively good by international standards.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, Prof Irene Ng's study based on 2002 data concluded that 58% of the income advantage of Singapore parents was being handed down to their children – a level similar to the USA at that time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we cannot measure how well we are doing, we cannot know how to make things better.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Mr Chairman, Enabling Masterplan 2 comes to fruition by the end of this year.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Notwithstanding its plans and progress, there is a sense on the ground that the majority of the public are still largely unaware of its achievements and undertakings, even the existence of the five-year Plan itself.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Page: 92 A friend told me that in her evening walks with her husband, she sometimes sees a person on a wheelchair at the bus-stop, where he would alight from a double-decker bus.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: He would wait patiently to ask for help from random passers-by to wheel him home.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: My friend's husband wheeled him one particular evening and, even for a young man in his 30s, it was not the easiest task.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: The 20-minute journey, gradually uphill, and made longer due to detours made inevitable by steps.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Imagine the man on a wheelchair having to ask for this favour almost every night.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: First, let us do help each other along, whether it is a man on a wheelchair or an old neighbour with dementia.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Second, I would like to sound a note for practical help.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Too often, the term "community help" means the Government leaving us to our own devices.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: This is great for those of us who have devices, but the Government needs to help those who cannot help themselves and to do so without eroding their dignity and self-worth.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Can the Minister also recap what are the key areas of progress made under Enabling Masterplan 2 and how the Government plans to build on these achievements?

text: Beyond continuing work on early intervention, I think we need to also give more support to families in caregiving for such groups and improving the service delivery and quality.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Can the Minister spell out the key focus areas of Enabling Masterplan 3?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Those of us who have been following the development of the special needs landscape in Singapore know that much has been achieved in the last decade.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The first salvo to include those with disabilities was launched by Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong when he was inaugurated.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: His inauguration speech set the tone and momentum of things to come.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Singaporeans should visit the SG Enable Village to see the dignity and support given to persons with special needs who might be suitable to work.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, we have amongst us in Parliament, a respected Nominated Member of Parliament, Ms Chia Yong Yong, a lawyer with peroneal muscular atrophy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have personally witnessed the quiet, commendable efforts made by the Parliament staff to ensure this Chamber and even our restroom facilities are accessible to Yong Yong.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These are exciting times for the special needs community.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But they are also alarming Page: 93 times, judging from the fast pace and ways by which technology can disrupt our world.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The directions laid down in Budget 2016 are just as relevant to this special community.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We must, as a country, address the community's near-term challenges.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, the special needs community, comprising Persons with Disabilities, their caregivers, the professionals, VWOs and other agencies, must be future-prepared.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They must acquire skills mastery in what they do.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They must attain innovation capability and learn to form enlightened partnerships in order to survive and, hopefully, thrive in the world of the future.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Dream big, dive deep, dare to deal with the difficult.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe that is the way to go.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore must dream big and cast the vision of fully embracing the special needs community as its rainbow to chase.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In every key aspect of life, Persons with Disabilities must be included, by default, in the main chapter of policymaking and not as an after-thought; or, worse, forgotten.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A Smart Nation is not so smart if it creates a digital divide between those who can and others who cannot or are not included to partake.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The SkillsFuture movement does not promise much of a future if it does not tangibly provide for those at risk of being left behind – the vulnerable, including Persons with Disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If lifelong learning is the way to go, then there is nothing to say that MOE's special schools cannot be resourced to become lifelong learning hubs so that persons with special needs can learn and contribute for life.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the special needs sector, we can leverage on our nation's advantage in technology to be the game changer to develop, scale and spread excellence so that more can benefit.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: To truly embrace the special needs community, the Government and other stakeholders must go beyond the usual general public consultations with focus groups in developing policies and programmes, especially for the upcoming Enabling Masterplan.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are several key disability types – intellectual, physical, developmental, sensory, learning – and groups with multiple disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Persons with Disabilities and their caregivers are not all the same in the issues they face.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are different levels of challenges, commitment, abilities and excellence amongst the service providers and agencies supporting them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to do more than ground sensing.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The usual general frustrations and disappointments will surface, but dive deeper we must, if we wish to excel.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Encourage each major disability group to study their own terrain and derive a mini Enabling Masterplan that highlights the pivotal needs of their charges, prioritise them, identify the gaps and recommend solutions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government must invite and study these plans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We know that not everything can be addressed by the Government, but it can surely play the role of Integrator and Facilitator to identify partners who can co-source or co-develop innovative solutions to address this area of growth or Page: 94 pains.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Singapore Association for the Deaf has attempted a mini-Enabling Masterplan highlighting the needs for effective early intervention.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Other deaf activists have raised the need to make captioning and sub-titling a default feature for all key national communications.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The adults who are visually impaired need a greater variety of jobs so that more of them can find work.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: More must be done upstream to train them and find jobs beyond the respected traditional professions like masseurs and buskers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The autism community has organised itself, formed the Autism Network Singapore and is in the process of developing its own Enabling Masterplan.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Their worry is also for the adults in their midst.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Just because someone is able to physically dress himself and go to the toilet independently does not mean he does not need supervision in other key aspects of life.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: To achieve excellence, the Government and all of us in the sector need to go beyond threading water and dive deeper.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Lastly, we must dare to deal with the difficult issues confronting the special needs community.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There may be no easy solutions for some of these issues and that is precisely the reason why we need to surface them, alert the relevant agencies and tap on the rest of the Singapore family.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Regular health screening and consultations by doctors, dentists and even optomologists capable of treating Persons with Disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Dr Chen Shiling from the Happee Hearts Movement has a vision of starting a specialised health centre for People with Disabilities (PWDs).

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They need the support of the rest of us.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Family caregivers who are emotionally at risk of taking their own lives and those of their children with special needs – they need help.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How can the Government and the rest of Singapore support them?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to dare to confront these difficult challenges.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Page: 95 Persons with special needs are more than their diagnosis.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They are not simply the objects of our charity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Someday, many of us may join this club when we lose our sight, our hearing and our mobility.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some of us may even lose our mental capacity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The only way to predict the future is to help create it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us dream big, dive deep and dare to deal with the difficult.

text: We worry about our children, our parents and our loved ones.

text: All the more, when such children, parents or loved ones have special needs, disabilities, illnesses or are in other ways vulnerable.

text: When we are not here anymore, what will happen to them?

text: With smaller families and an ageing population, there are fewer family members to share the caregiving role.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Many caregivers of persons with disabilities are elderly parents, who, in no time, will no longer be able to continue in their caregiving roles.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Caregivers of elderly parents, spouses or siblings with disabilities will also grow older.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In the vicissitudes of life, some of us will not survive the ones that we take care of.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We do not want to leave our loved ones to charity; neither do we want to burden the state unnecessarily.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, almost all sectors compete for manpower from the same limited pool.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Ironically, even as the economy slows, many organisations still cannot fully meet their hiring needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Social spending has been rising steadily for a number of years now and it has required sectors, such as social and family services, to increase their demand for manpower at a time when the supply is tight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: From childcare centres to old-age care, the rate of increase in Government spending and the urgency of meeting certain performance targets are occurring at a pace faster than we had seen in the past.

text: Please allow me to point to three specific areas of concern.

text: Even if manpower were more readily available, proper training and deployment take time.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Before my involvement in the social services sector, I took the view that social service professionals served out of passion and therefore, should expect a pay cut, compared to their peers in other sectors.

text: I also took the view that my donations, however paltry, should go to direct services to beneficiaries and not towards the administration of the charity.

text: I did not realise then how wrong I was.

text: We should not penalise anyone for serving out of passion.

text: We should remember that they have families to feed, children and loved ones whom they wish to provide for.

text: They have aspirations and, if they leave the sector to fulfil those legitimate aspirations, our beneficiaries will suffer.

text: I did not realise that for a VWO to help their beneficiaries effectively, it must run well as a whole organisation.

text: Corporate support functions and good governance are important.

text: We need good professionals and staff to manage and operate corporate support, to implement good governance, in order for our therapists, social workers and counsellors to serve and support our beneficiaries effectively.

text: However, VWOs encounter challenges in some of this funding and I would like to share some of them.

text: An example would be the Innovation and Productivity Grant.

text: Having stated the above, I do want to acknowledge that the current two-year Corporate Development Fund Scheme is a good start.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Specifically, for this debate, I would like to ask if the Government would be able to streamline and simplify the criteria and the process for the application of Government grants.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Chairman, I would like to start off my speech by providing an overview of my Ministry's focus in Mandarin before resuming in English.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: (In Mandarin):   The continual progress and prosperity of a country depend not just on a strong economy; it is equally important that we build an inclusive society and help Singaporeans build a caring home.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: MSF will be working on three priorities moving forward.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Our first priority is to make Singapore a good home for the family and for every child to have a good start in life, regardless of family background.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Strong and happy families are the basic building blocks of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Our families are what make life meaningful for us.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This will not be just an MSF effort, but a whole-of-Government priority.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: For each of our families and for Singapore as a whole, our children are our future.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We want them to grow up in strong families and a safe and nurturing environment.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: For children who have less, we will give them an extra leg up, so that they, too, will have the opportunity to live to their potential and to chase rainbows.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Hence, we are providing greater support to families with young children.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: MSF will continue to expand accessible, affordable and quality early childhood education.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The children's early years are essential to their physical and mental development and will have a long-term impact on their future.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This new initiative will proactively identify vulnerable families and children through various indicators, so as to provide them with early access to the necessary health, learning and developmental support.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We will also provide parents with the knowledge and skills to care for and support their children's development.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Our second priority is to continue to strengthen our social safety net and improve the lives of the low-income and more vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We are aware that the cost of living is high in Singapore and that our low-income households have to grapple with it every day.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: As the Minister for Finance has mentioned in his Budget speech, we are increasing the cash assistance for those on ComCare long-term assistance.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Page: 99 The ComCare Long Term Assistance scheme is a package of assistance for those who are permanently unable to work due to reasons, such as old-age or disability, and have little savings and family support.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The assistance will also be increased for larger households.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Besides cash assistance, they will also continue to receive free medical care and additional assistance.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Many of them are also allocated heavily subsidised HDB rental flats.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: At the same time, we will also do more for Persons with Disabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: However, I would like to stress that to be a truly inclusive society, relying on Government subsidies or policies alone is not enough.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We would need the wider community to step forward and play a part in improving the lives of those among us who are weaker.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This would be MSF's third priority − building a caring society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We will continue to support VWOs to raise their capabilities and help social service professionals develop themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: At the same time, NCSS will also work with our VWOs to expand volunteerism opportunities, so that Singaporeans and businesses who are keen to contribute to society can do so.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This will encourage corporations and the communities to contribute to society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Only by caring and supporting one another can we march towards the next 50 years.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: I hope that in 50 years' time, Singapore will not be successful just economically, but equally outstanding in having a more cohesive and caring society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: It is a vision that needs each and every one of us to realise.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: (In English): Chairman, when we speak of people being Singapore's only resource, many think we are just referring to the Singaporean worker, how educated he is, how hard-working, how skilled.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: In short, how he can contribute to keeping Singapore going for the next bound.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: But in reality, the Singaporean is no less a father, husband, son, mother, daughter or wife.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The Singaporean lives within a delicate web of human ties, a network which I know each of us in this House seeks to help make stronger and more meaningful.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: As we begin our journey over the next 50 years, it is important for us to take stock and remember what we aspire for Singapore – a land of opportunity where citizens can realise their dreams.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Dreams take root and have meaning only within the precious network of meaningful relationships and bonds, of strong families and good friends, of an inclusive and caring society, across all races and all religions.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: For individuals, it can be by fiat of birth, by force of circumstance, by exercise of rational choice or by a chance chemistry of mutual attraction.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: On a larger scale, we all know our population is ageing.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Ours is an economic age of volatility and uncertainty, and social needs, therefore, are becoming more varied, complex and Page: 100 multi-faceted.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Our family laws are changing to reflect these new realities.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Unfortunately, today, we are more likely to divorce each other than before.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We have a more diverse architecture in life choices even as parenting becomes a constant battle of school stresses and social media temptations and distractions.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Against these social facts, what cards do we have to play?

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We are only as strong as the values we hold dear.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: And they are: that everyone − rich or poor − should have the same shot at success.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: That we value individual effort and strong families.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: And last, that we are all in this together: Equal Opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: These are enduring values which my Ministry will seek to uphold in our work for this term of Government.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: And in terms of how we intend to carry out our work, I hope to go upstream where we can.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Strong families are, and must remain, the basic building blocks of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Strong marriages form the foundation for strong families.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We do want to create a pro-family environment, which supports couples' decision to settle down, have children and enjoy family life.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We will strengthen marriages and families so that family members maintain strong ties with one another and with the community.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: For each of our families and our society, children are our future.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: With strong families and good support from society, our children can have a good start in life.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We have helped persons with disabilities to lead more independent lives and realise their potential.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We will work with different Ministries to deliver more coordinated help to those with varied needs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: My Parliamentary Secretary will speak on how we will help the low-income, the vulnerable seniors and youths-at-risk.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: He will also outline how we will continue to support and empower persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Thirdly, it is also very much about enabling Caring Communities.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Building an inclusive society with a strong sense of "we", as opposed to "me", is very much our collective aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This came across strongly during Our Singapore Conversations and even in the present ongoing SGFuture series of dialogues.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: To be a truly inclusive society, we need more than strong Government safety nets.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We need a wider community which has the heart and the will to play a part in improving the lives of those among us who are weaker, have less or have fallen on hard times.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: When we talk about an inclusive society, it is not just about including those who need help or who need the support.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: It is about all of us being included in that whole journey.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The positive outcomes of such actions are not, and I repeat, are not limited to the beneficiaries.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The change also occurs for those who give of their time, energy and resources.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Helping others brings out our humanity as individuals and strengthens our common identity as Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: For this first speech, let me share some of our upcoming work in building our home for family and to provide a good start for our children.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Our families are what make life meaningful for us.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: They are our pillar of support in good and bad times.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Strong family bonds need to be nurtured and forged through the quality and quantity of time spent together.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We all know that when both parents are involved at home and with their children's lives, marital relationships are stronger.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Children thrive when parental relationships are positive, when they are loved by their parents, grandparents and other family members.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Ageing parents also thrive when their adult children, their siblings and other family members are supportive.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: In the coming years, my Ministry will continue to strengthen these fundamental family relationships.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Where relationships are intact, we work towards reinforcing them further.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Where relationships have problems, we try to help repair and preserve them.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Where they have invariably broken down, as it tends to happen sometimes, we will try to minimise the negative impact.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Central to our work here are the interest of the children and their development.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: My Ministry supports and provides marriage preparation programmes and counselling through our network of partners.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We equip couples with skills, such as communications and conflict management, to prepare them for the ups and downs of marriage life.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We also work with the Families for Life Council on bonding activities for families to promote family time among extended families and on the Marriage Convention which also provides useful tips for couples to enrich their marriage.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: For couples who may face more stresses in their marriage life, we have put in place many other targeted programmes, like those for couples who married young and those for marriages involving a foreign spouse.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We do encourage Members in this House to encourage others to take on-board all this range of programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We all know, as new parents, we will face anxiety and stress.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Will we be able to handle the sleepless nights when baby comes?

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Who will take care of our little one when we are out at work?

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: What are the major expenses involved in raising a child?

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: These are very valid and practical questions that I think all of us have asked.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: I remember asking them myself when I first became a parent.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Page: 102 Today, we have a suite of support measures covering various life stages – from getting married to having and raising children and providing support for working parents.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: I, for one, do not believe that couples have children just because of campaigns or to benefit from the grants and schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: But I do believe that our policies, collectively, can help create a conducive environment and climate to support couples who do want to become parents, who do want to settle down and who do want to have more children.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Going forward, we want to do more to facilitate early bonding between parents and newborns.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We also want to give new parents greater support and encourage more to get into the habit of saving for their children's future.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: You may already have heard about plans to enhance paternity leave.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The Minister for Finance has also announced the new CDA First Step.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: These initiatives are part of our support for marriage and parenthood.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: And I will leave it to Senior Minister of State Josephine Teo to give you details of these and other initiatives during NPTD's Committee of Supply.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: As a parent myself, I know that parenting is more challenging today.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: In this age when social media and the Internet bring outside influences straight to our young children in a very unfiltered fashion, we need to be even more vigilant and play a more active role to ensure that our children are exposed to the right values.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This is where we, as parents, must play our part.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: To help parents, we have implemented two parenting programmes in schools – the Positive Parenting Programme and the Signposts programme.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: A local study in 2010 found that first-time fathers who were more involved in caring for the young infants, adjusted better to fatherhood.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Yet, in many families, as Mr Seah Kian Peng pointed out, mothers continue to carry the greater responsibility in child-raising.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We need to encourage fathers to step forward, but I think times are also beginning to change and I see fathers getting more hands-on.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Naturally, we see fathers carrying their babies, feeding them and, especially in the libraries, you see them reading to their children.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The children are quite safe with you, so do step forward.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: In 2009, my Ministry started the Dads for Life movement.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The Centre for Fathering is now driving the effort, with our support, to expand outreach to the community, schools and workplaces.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Dads for Life ambassadors are also reaching out to childcare centres and Primary schools to encourage fathers to be more active dads through a strong network of father support groups.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: A 2013 MSF survey showed that six in 10 men polled responded that their job kept them from spending more time with their families.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: In recent years, we have introduced paternity and shared parental leave to give fathers more time with their children right from birth.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Fathers are also eligible for childcare leave which applies to older children, too.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We have talked about this in previous Committees of Supply.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: And with most of us being working parents, Mr Christopher de Souza and Ms Page: 103 Thanaletchimi were right to point out that the workplace needs to be pro-family as well.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Today, the Work-Life Grant co-funds lactation facilities in offices.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: It also incentivises employers to provide flexible work arrangements, which are sought after by men, too, as shown by a 2014 survey conducted by The Straits Times and the Employer Alliance.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: I call on employers to embrace these measures to support fathers and mothers as well.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We can pass all the policies, initiatives and incentives but, ultimately, we need to walk that last step.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: While we are committed to working with the community and employers to support active fathering, the final step has to be taken by the fathers themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Many of you would agree with me that time is precious.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: As a father myself, I find that time is fleeting.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Sometimes, I will pop into their rooms to chat with them before they sleep.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Where we can, we play board games or, sometimes, sit in front of the computer to share our favourite Jimmy Fallon episodes or Saturday Night Live.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This is not very strategic but I think we have a great time together just joking and laughing and I think whatever we can do, let us just take the effort to try to be there and to be present.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: For fathers, particularly, our presence is a lot more critical than we realise in terms of the long-term impact on our children.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: As we support active parenting, it is also important for us to help parents provide a good start for their children.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The early years, we all know, are when our children develop language competencies, habits and socio-emotional skills that provide the foundation for their future.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: What we want is for parents to have access to affordable and good quality early childhood services.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We have made significant investments to level up the early childhood sector.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about our progress and our next steps.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: I am very aware that demand remains high in certain estates with concentrations of parents with young children, a point which Ms Sun Xueling has raised.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Just to share, childcare places in Punggol and Sengkang have increased by more than 60% in just the last three years, to 13,000 places today.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: But as we expand capacity, it is important for us to assure parents that their children are well-looked after.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: First, there are now more centres certified by the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) under the Singapore Preschool Accreditation Framework (SPARK).

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This helps parents choose a quality preschool for their child.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Page: 104 Second, we will introduce a new Early Childhood Development Centres Act later this year.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
